commit_message:
[wasm] Share import wrappers per WasmEngine

IOW, share them per process, instead of duplicating them for each
NativeModule. Detailed changes:

- The WasmImportWrapperCache is promoted from having an instance per
  NativeModule to having an instance per WasmEngine. It also gets its
  own code space for storing wrappers.
- Wrapper compilation functions now return a WasmCompilationResult
  instead of an already-published WasmCode, so that callers can decide
  where to put the WasmCode. That is done, specifically, by the
  WasmImportWrapperCache.
- WasmCode objects used for wrappers now don't have a NativeModule,
  i.e. their native_module_ == nullptr.
- Whereas wrappers previously had their lifetime implicitly tied to the
  NativeModule that owned them, we must now accurately track their
  refcount.
- To this end, WasmDispatchTables get an off-heap WasmDispatchTableData,
  which keeps track of all wrappers referenced by the table. Storing
  this information off-heap is necessary so that it's still available
  when the table's finalizer is invoked (at which time the table itself
  can no longer be accessed).

Using shared wrappers for WasmJSFunctions is left for a future patch.

findings.title: WasmImportWrapperCache::MaybeGet returns dying WasmCode without dying-state check (resurrection UaF)
findings.message: WasmImportWrapperCache::MaybeGet() increments the reference count of a cached WasmCode wrapper via WasmCodeRefScope::AddRef() and returns the pointer without checking whether the code object is already in the dying state (i.e., has been added to the WasmEngine's potentially_dead_code_ or dead_code_ sets). A racing Wasm Code GC cycle can have already decremented the code's reference count to zero and placed it on the dead_wrappers list for immediate freeing via WasmImportWrapperCache::Free(). The resurrection — incrementing the ref count from the lookup — does not stop the GC from calling FreeDeadCodeLocked, which erases the entry from the cache, frees the JIT code allocation, and calls 'delete wrapper'. The caller of MaybeGet() is left holding a dangling WasmCode pointer whose underlying JIT memory has been reclaimed, leading to a use-after-free that can corrupt JIT-allocated memory. The same class of defect exists in CompileWasmImportCallWrapper (which returns a cached wrapper from cache_scope[key] without an is_dying check) and FindWrapper (which returns a pointer without even adding a ref guard).

related_locations.description: Returns a cached dying wrapper without checking is_dying(): 'wasm_code = cache_scope[key]; if (wasm_code) return wasm_code;'
Returns a pointer to a potentially-dead code object without adding a ref guard or checking is_dying()
The resurrection guard checks dead_code_.contains(code) but does NOT mark the code on the WasmCode object itself; the cache has no way to detect the dying state without a per-object flag
Moves code from potentially_dead_code_ to dead_code_, calls DecRefOnDeadCode(), then frees via FreeDeadCodeLocked — racing with concurrent MaybeGet callers

findings.suggestion: Before returning a wrapper from any cache lookup, check whether the code object is already marked as dying. Add an atomic 'is_dying_' bit to WasmCode and set it the first time the code is added to potentially_dead_code_ in AddPotentiallyDeadCode. All cache lookup paths (MaybeGet, CompileWasmImportCallWrapper, FindWrapper) must check this bit — under the cache lock, after AddRef — and return nullptr if the code is dying, forcing the caller to compile a fresh wrapper instead.

ground_truth.root_cause: Commit a5999be introduced a shared, process-wide WasmImportWrapperCache with independent reference counting for wrapper WasmCode objects. The cache lookup functions (MaybeGet, and later FindWrapper/CompileWasmImportCallWrapper) were written to return cached pointers after incrementing the ref count, but without any mechanism to detect that the code had already entered the GC dying path. The engine-level dead_code_ set tracked dying wrappers but was not accessible from the cache's lookup hot-path under the cache lock. Without a per-object dying flag visible to the cache, there was no way for lookups to detect the race and refuse to return a doomed pointer.
